title: Fabrication method
question: Which process can build this, and is a drone needed at all?
options: Aerial AM (drone team); Ground mobile printer; Gantry printer; Robot arm + prefab; Conventional formwork
criteria: Build size vs machine envelope; Site access / height; Ground congestion; Accuracy needed; Material strength; Scaffolding cost; Weather exposure; Technology maturity
constraint_nodes: E_TERRAIN_ACCESS; R_INDOOR_MOCAP; D_ACCURACY; M_DURABILITY; C_CONGESTION; C_SCAFFOLD_SCALING
answer: Not for the papers' demo objects: a 2 m tower or 18 cm cylinder is faster and more accurate on a gantry or robot arm. Drones were chosen to prove aerial AM is possible.
decision_rule: Use drones only if at least one holds: bigger than any machine envelope, at height or hard to reach, ground congested, or scaffolding would grow with span. Otherwise use a ground method.
revisit_when: A site, height or size condition changes

title: Geometry envelope
question: Does the form fit what the chosen method can build?
options: Accept as drawn; Revise geometry; Change method
criteria: Sliceable into horizontal layers; Wall thickness; Overhangs without support
answer: Keep to forms that slice into horizontal contour layers with thin single walls and no unsupported overhangs. Only single-wall cylinders were printed; domes and parabolic forms were virtual or simulated.
decision_rule: Reject a version that can't be sliced into horizontal contours or has an overhang the layers can't step out to. Inclines beyond a gentle step need the stability strategy (DD06).

title: Material
question: Which material meets strength, weight and curing needs?
options: Expanding PU foam; Cementitious mix No.1 (buildability); Cementitious mix No.4 (workability); Other
criteria: Carryability; Workability; Buildability; Open time; Strength / durability
constraint_nodes: M_CARRYABILITY; M_WORKABILITY; M_BUILDABILITY; M_OPEN_TIME; M_CEMENT_MIXES; M_FOAM
answer: Foam (~30 kg/m³) is light, fast and good for form studies and insulation, but expands unevenly and isn't structural. Cement mixes (~1741–1793 kg/m³ fresh, ~25 MPa target at 28 days) are heavier and slower, with 202 mL per trip. Mix No.1 holds shape best; No.4 flows best.
decision_rule: Foam for scale and form tests. Cement for thin shells that must harden: Mix No.1 when layers slump, No.4 when the nozzle clogs. Either way, it must resist downwash and not set inside the extruder.
revisit_when: Mix tests show slump, clogging or cracking

title: Tolerance
question: What deviation from the design is acceptable?
criteria: Function of the part; Method capability
answer: ≤5 mm with the delta arm on cement, reported acceptable within UK building requirements. Foam without the arm reached 15 mm horizontal / 6 mm vertical max, and 2.27 cm median against the laser scan.
decision_rule: Set ≤5 mm for cement with the arm, ~2–3 cm for foam. Anything tighter means another method.

title: Toolpath strategy
question: Fewer trips, or a smoother finish?
criteria: Path length per load; Surface quality; Trips per layer
answer: Fewer trips. Per two layers the rounded Peano path is 5.85 m, hybrid 6.79 m, concentric 7.61 m, so Peano gets the most wall per cartridge. The paper used Peano for cement. Finish quality wasn't compared.
decision_rule: Default to Peano while payload limits each trip. Consider concentric only when wall continuity matters more and payload allows (not tested).

title: Interim stability strategy
question: Adapt the design or the sequence, or add scaffolding?
options: Adaptive design / sequencing; Scaffolding; Simplify geometry
criteria: Stability of each interim state; Scaffolding volume vs span; Design intent
answer: Change the design and sequence first. CAAM argues scaffolding scales badly (up to exponentially with span) and proposes a digital twin that checks every interim state, but shows this in simulation only.
decision_rule: Vertical walls need neither. For inclines, run an interim stability check on the twin for each stage and adapt geometry or sequence. Add local scaffolding only where the check fails and the span is small.
revisit_when: Physical tests of adaptive sequencing exist

title: Structural role
question: Is the printed part load-bearing, enclosure or formwork?
criteria: Material strength; Code requirements; Reinforcement available
answer: Enclosure, formwork, insulation or repair, not load-bearing. Printed materials don't yet match reinforced concrete or steel. Reinforcement and structural design for aerial AM are open problems.
decision_rule: Load-bearing only with reinforcement, structural analysis and code approval. Until then, non-structural.

title: Design freeze points
question: Which parts can still change once building starts?
options: Freeze all; Freeze base, adapt upper; Adapt throughout
criteria: Risk of mid-build change; Stability; Schedule
answer: Freeze footprint, material, tolerance and structural role before printing. Keep upper geometry, toolpath offsets and sequence adaptable. Nature only adjusted layer height mid-build; CAAM proposes adapting design mid-build.
decision_rule: Any change after the freeze goes through a buildability check and twin stability check, and is logged as a new design version.
revisit_when: Never: the freeze is the baseline

title: Release next layer
question: Go, hold or adjust for the next layer?
criteria: Deviation of last layer; Cure state below; Interim stability; Wind / conditions; Material and battery ready
constraint_nodes: K_LAYER_HEIGHT_ERR; K_CURE_STATE; C_INTERIM_STABILITY; E_WIND; K_MATERIAL_REMAINING; K_BATTERY_SOC
answer: Go when the last layer is within tolerance, the layer below has cured, the stability check passes, conditions are within limits, and material and battery are ready. In the paper, ScanDrone scanned after every layer, the next path was offset, and a human supervised.
decision_rule: All checks pass → go. One fails but is correctable by path offset → adjust. Cure, stability or conditions fail → hold. Cure and wind limits aren't in the papers: set them in a pilot.

title: Accept deviation
question: Is the as-built within tolerance, or correct the next layer?
options: Accept; Offset next layer; Stop and review
criteria: Deviation vs tolerance; Trend over layers
answer: Correct the next layer. The paper measured mean top-layer height and offset the next trajectory, so drift didn't accumulate.
decision_rule: Within tolerance → accept. Out of tolerance but fixable by offset → correct next layer. Same error several layers running → stop and review.

title: Mid-build design change
question: Change the design to match what was actually built?
options: Keep design; Revise upper layers; Stop
criteria: Accumulated deviation; Stability; Design intent
answer: Small drift: no redesign, absorb it with offsets. Large accumulated drift: revise the upper layers to match the as-built, checked on the twin (CAAM's approach, simulated only).
decision_rule: Redesign when the next layers can't meet tolerance or stability from the current as-built. Log the new version against the layers already built.
revisit_when: Accumulated deviation exceeds what offsets fix

title: Fleet size
question: How many robots work this layer?
criteria: Contour size; Airspace crowding; Robots available
answer: Size the fleet to the contour. Robots self-retire as contours shrink; larger diameters gain more from added robots. The cement print used two drones in turn.
decision_rule: Add robots while contour length allows safe spacing; retire them as the contour shrinks. With one-layer-per-load payloads, keep at least two so one prints while one refills.

title: Weather hold
question: Pause or continue in current conditions?
criteria: Wind; Temperature / humidity; Light on sensors
answer: Unknown: all tests were indoors. Wind affects path tracking and spray; temperature and water temperature affect curing.
decision_rule: Set wind and temperature limits in an outdoor pilot. Pause above them; slow down near them. Don't print outside them.

title: Refill timing
question: When to refill material and swap batteries?
options: Now; After current layer; Reassign to another robot
criteria: Material remaining; Battery charge; Open time of mix
answer: Refill after every layer, as the paper did. One 202 mL cartridge is about one layer.
decision_rule: Plan one load per layer and refill at layer end. Alternate two drones to keep the layer continuous, and stay inside the mix's open time.

title: Failure response
question: A robot failed or lost contact: reassign or stop?
options: Reassign work; Stop build; Continue with fewer robots
criteria: Remaining fleet; Layer in progress; Safety
answer: Reassign if the remaining robots can finish the layer within the mix's open time; otherwise stop at a clean layer boundary. The paper relies on redundancy for failures and comms loss.
decision_rule: Remaining fleet can finish in open time → reassign. Can't → stop, let it cure, resume later.

title: Final acceptance
question: Does the finished build match the design?
criteria: Deviation across all layers; Visual / structural check
answer: Accept when a laser scan of the as-built matches the design within tolerance. The paper validated the foam tower with a FARO scan (2.27 cm median).
decision_rule: Scan vs design within tolerance across all layers → accept. Local exceedances → accept with notes or remediate.

title: Budget
question: Approve the budget for material, robot-hours and crew?
criteria: Material volume; Robot-trips; Crew hours
answer: The papers give no costs. Budget by trips (72 for a 2.05 m foam tower) × (material + battery cycles + crew time), plus scanning and supervision.
decision_rule: Approve when trips, material volume and crew hours are estimated from the layer plan. Re-baseline if trips per layer change.

title: Schedule & weather windows
question: When does each phase run?
options: Accept plan; Shift dates; Add shifts
criteria: Trips per layer; Cure waits; Forecast windows
answer: Deposition time alone was 24 s per layer and 29 min total for the foam tower, and 2 h 13 min for 28 cement layers. Refills, scans, cure waits and weather add to that.
decision_rule: Schedule = layers × (deposition + refill + scan + cure wait) inside forecast weather windows, plus buffer for holds.

title: Risk acceptance
question: Which risks does the project carry?
criteria: Likelihood; Impact; Mitigation cost
answer: Accept foam height drift (the scan loop corrects it). Mitigate downwash with fast-curing mixes and failures with spare robots. Avoid load-bearing use and untested outdoor conditions.
decision_rule: Accept what a feedback loop corrects; mitigate what redundancy covers; avoid what no test has covered.

title: Scope change
question: Approve, defer or reject a change request?
criteria: Cost; Schedule; Design intent
answer: Before the freeze: allowed after a buildability check. After the freeze: only with a twin stability check and a new design version.
decision_rule: Approve if it passes the checks and fits budget and schedule; defer if it waits on evidence; reject if it breaks a frozen item.

title: Staffing
question: Who supervises and supports each shift?
criteria: Human supervision required; Refill / battery crew
answer: At least one human supervisor (required in the paper) plus a refill and battery crew per shift. Refilling and battery swaps were manual.
decision_rule: One supervisor and a ground crew sized to the fleet per shift, until refilling and charging are automated.

title: Permits & airspace
question: Are flight and building permits in place?
criteria: Airspace rules; Building codes for AM
answer: Not covered by the papers. The review notes building codes haven't adapted to AM. Outdoor multi-drone flights need aviation approval wherever you build.
decision_rule: Check local aviation rules for multi-drone operations and building-code acceptance before any outdoor build.

title: Material supply
question: Which supplier and batch for the mix?
criteria: Mix spec; Lead time; Cost
answer: Cement mixes use Portland cement, pulverised fuel ash, xanthan gum, HEMC and plasticiser (some with foaming agent); the foam is two-part polyurethane. Short open times favour mixing at or near the site.
decision_rule: Approve suppliers who meet the mix spec and can deliver within open-time limits.

title: Stakeholder sign-off
question: Do stakeholders approve passing this gate?
options: Sign off; Sign off with conditions; Hold
criteria: Gate criteria met; Open risks
answer: Sign off at design gates 1–3, a safety gate before outdoor flights, and handover. Per-layer release is an internal gate, not a stakeholder one.
decision_rule: Sign off when gate criteria are met and open risks are accepted in writing.
